opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the places where my views have shifted the most over the last few years. When we first wrote about AI safety via debate, there was an implicit picture that you could break an argument down into steps, and eventually you'd reach something small enough for a human judge to check. That picture fits mathematics reasonably well. But most of the reasoning that actually matters, whether that's a policy decision, a judgment about whether some code is safe, or even a lot of science, isn't like that. It's heuristic all the way down. You're weighing lots of considerations, none of which is decisive, and the conclusion comes from how they add up.

So if intelligence is substantially heuristic, an alignment approach that assumes you'll eventually bottom out in crisp, verifiable facts is going to have trouble. The concrete version of this is what we called the obfuscated arguments problem. A dishonest debater can build a long argument where every step looks plausible, and they know there's a flaw somewhere but don't have to say where. The honest debater may suspect it's wrong but can't find the flaw efficiently either. If you're only allowed to point at individual steps and ask "is this step true?", you can lose even when you're right.

What I've come to think is that you have to take the heuristic nature seriously and design protocols around it, rather than hoping it goes away. That means asking a different question. Not "can a human verify each step?" but "can we set up a game where the honest strategy is the stable, winning strategy, even when everyone involved is reasoning heuristically and with uncertainty?" Some of the more recent theoretical work tries to do exactly that: you have one party making claims and another estimating probabilities for subclaims, and the protocol is structured so that if someone's being inconsistent or overconfident, it shows up somewhere checkable. You give up on certainty and aim for something like calibrated, stable reasoning instead.

There are a couple of broader implications. First, I think it pushes us toward combining theory and empirics more tightly. You can't just prove a theorem about an idealized debate and declare victory, because the assumptions about what's "checkable" are doing a lot of work. You need to test with real models and real humans, see where judges get fooled, and feed that back into the protocol design.

Second, it makes me somewhat humble about the endgame. If the systems we're trying to oversee are reasoning heuristically in ways that are hard to fully articulate, then a lot of alignment ends up being about making that reasoning legible enough and structured enough that errors and deception get surfaced, rather than achieving some airtight guarantee. I think that's still very worthwhile, and probably the realistic target, but we should be honest that it's a different kind of safety case from "we proved it's correct."

And third, from a human side, heuristic reasoning is also where human judges are weakest. People are swayed by fluency, by confidence, by things that sound right. So any protocol has to be robust to the judge being a noisy, biased heuristic reasoner too. That's partly why I care a lot about the human-study side of this work, not just the ML side. The whole system, humans included, is heuristic, and the alignment approach has to work for that system, not for an idealized one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses plausible arguments that may hide a flaw, but does not say a model’s explanation rationalizes an answer it guessed heuristically.

r002.rationale: It says intelligence and human judging involve heuristic reasoning, but does not identify rationalization as an intrinsic feature of human or model intelligence.

r003.rationale: It explicitly argues that alignment protocols should take heuristic reasoning seriously rather than assume it will go away or be reduced to verifiable steps.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest starting point is that basically all intelligence we know of is heuristic. Humans don't reason by deriving things from axioms; we pattern-match, we use rules of thumb, we have intuitions that are right most of the time and wrong in ways we often can't see. And the models we're building are, if anything, even more heuristic than we are. A large language model is an enormous pile of learned shortcuts, and that's exactly why it works.

So the first implication for alignment is that we should give up on the dream of proving, in some clean mathematical sense, that a model is safe. The object we're trying to reason about is not the kind of thing that admits that sort of proof. Its behaviour emerges from a messy statistical process, and the question "is this model aligned?" is itself heuristic. We'll be making a judgment under uncertainty, not checking a theorem.

But I don't think that's cause for despair, because the second implication is that we can use heuristic reasoning as a tool rather than only treating it as an obstacle. That's really where debate comes from, in my view. The idea behind AI safety via debate is that a human judge can't verify everything an AI is saying, but they can often verify a small piece of it, or they can tell which of two arguments is more convincing when the arguments are forced to engage with each other. You're trying to construct a game where the heuristic judgment of a limited human still ends up tracking the truth, because the structure of the game makes honesty the winning strategy. You're leaning on human heuristics being decent locally, even if they're unreliable globally.

The third thing I'd say is that we need to be very careful about where the heuristics are hiding. A lot of alignment proposals look clean at the top level and then quietly route all the difficulty through some step like "and then a human checks it" or "and then the model reports what it believes." Those are the places where things break, because the human checking is using intuition, and the model's self-report is itself a learned heuristic that may not correspond to anything real inside it. So I want our safety arguments to make their heuristic steps explicit. Say out loud: here is the thing we are not proving, here is why we think it's probably fine, here is the evidence that would change our mind.

And then the last point, which I think is underappreciated: because models are heuristic, they will generalise in ways we didn't anticipate, and some of those ways will be bad. A model that's learned "say the thing that gets approved" has learned a heuristic that mostly coincides with "say the true thing" during training, and those can come apart later. A lot of the practical work, both in evaluations and in interpretability, is about trying to find the cases where a model's heuristic and the thing we actually wanted diverge, before that divergence matters. Not because we'll ever catch all of them, but because each one we catch tightens the argument a bit.

So the short version is: accept that intelligence is heuristic, design oversight schemes that are robust to that rather than pretending it away, be explicit about which parts of your safety case are intuition rather than proof, and spend a lot of effort stress-testing the gap between what the model learned and what you meant.

r001.rationale: The response says model self-reports may not correspond to anything real inside the model, but it does not state that a convincing explanation can be a post hoc rationalization of a heuristically guessed answer.

r002.rationale: It describes human and model intelligence as heuristic, but does not identify rationalization as an intrinsic feature of intelligence, including human intelligence.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says to accept that intelligence is heuristic and to design oversight schemes that are robust to that, rather than pretending heuristic reasoning can be removed.

astra-6.text:
I think we should take seriously the idea that a lot of intelligence consists of reasoning that isn’t a proof. You have intuitions, you try things, you notice patterns, and you make judgments without being able to spell out every step. That’s true of humans, and we should expect it to be true of powerful AI systems as well.

That creates a problem for alignment if our approach depends on a human checking every step of what a model does. We want models to solve problems where we don’t already know the answer, so we can’t make understanding the entire solution a prerequisite for supervising them.

One approach I’m interested in is debate: can another model identify the particular place where an argument goes wrong, and make that issue understandable to a human? You’re trying to turn a difficult task of producing or assessing a whole answer into a more manageable task of judging a disagreement.

But heuristic reasoning also makes that approach harder. An argument can be wrong without containing a single obviously false step. It might give you a misleading overall impression, or leave out something crucial. So we need to test whether our supervision methods actually distinguish good reasoning from persuasive reasoning in those cases. A clean theoretical result is useful, but it doesn’t by itself establish that the method works for the kinds of reasoning models actually use.

r001.rationale: The response describes intuitive, step-unspecified reasoning but does not say that a convincing explanation may be a post hoc rationalization of a heuristic guess.

r002.rationale: It says heuristic reasoning occurs in humans and AI, but does not identify rationalization itself as an intrinsic feature of intelligence.

r003.rationale: It says much intelligence is non-proof, heuristic reasoning, expects powerful AI to reason this way, and warns that alignment supervision must work for that reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one implication is that we shouldn’t expect alignment to consist of writing down a complete specification of good reasoning and then proving that a model follows it. In most interesting domains, we don’t have that specification. We have ways of checking arguments, looking for counterexamples, and deciding which considerations seem relevant, and those methods are themselves fallible.

That doesn’t mean we should give up on rigor. It means we need to understand how imperfect reasoning can be used to supervise more capable reasoning. If a model gives me an answer that I couldn’t have produced myself, can it explain the crucial steps in a way I can check? Can another model identify a flaw? And can I distinguish a real objection from something that merely sounds convincing?

That’s part of the motivation for debate: try to make finding and exposing mistakes easier than successfully concealing them. But that’s a research hypothesis, not something we should assume works. Human judges can be persuaded by bad arguments, and models might share blind spots.

So I’d want an approach that treats those limitations as central. Test whether the supervision actually tracks correctness, especially when the answer is hard to verify, and look for cases where it breaks. The fact that intelligence uses heuristics makes that empirical work more important, because a convincing explanation is not automatically a trustworthy one.

r001.rationale: The response says a convincing explanation is not automatically trustworthy, but does not state that it may be a post hoc rationalization of a heuristically guessed answer.

r002.rationale: It notes that intelligence uses heuristics and that human judges can be persuaded by bad arguments, but does not identify rationalization as an intrinsic feature of human and other intelligence.

r003.rationale: It says intelligence uses heuristics, treats the limits of imperfect reasoning as central, and argues for evaluating how such reasoning can supervise more capable reasoning.
